reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: An autoimmune inflammatory infiltration of the pituitary that can mimic a pituitary adenoma both clinically and on imaging
Classically affects women in late pregnancy or the postpartum period, though it occurs in both sexes and other settings
Presenting features include headache, visual disturbance from mass effect, and variable hypopituitarism
A characteristic pattern is early and disproportionate loss of ACTH and TSH secretion, unlike the sequence often seen with compressive adenomas
Diabetes insipidus is relatively common when the infiltration involves the posterior pituitary or stalk (infundibuloneurohypophysitis)
MRI typically shows symmetrical pituitary enlargement with homogeneous enhancement and stalk thickening, helping distinguish it from adenoma
It is increasingly recognised as an adverse effect of immune checkpoint inhibitor cancer therapy
Management combines hormone replacement for deficient axes with anti-inflammatory therapy or surgery reserved for significant mass effect or diagnostic uncertainty
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphocytic hypophysitis is characterised by autoimmune lymphocytic and plasma-cell infiltration of the pituitary gland, causing inflammation, oedema, and enlargement that can compress adjacent structures and the gland itself. The inflammatory process impairs hormone-secreting cells, often affecting corticotrophs and thyrotrophs relatively early, and may extend to the stalk and posterior lobe to cause diabetes insipidus. Over time the gland may fibrose and atrophy, sometimes leaving an empty sella and permanent hypopituitarism. The condition is frequently associated with other autoimmune diseases and, increasingly, with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy that unmasks pituitary autoimmunity.
additionalDifferentials: Sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and other infiltrative or granulomatous disease of the pituitary
Langerhans cell histiocytosis and IgG4-related hypophysitis
additionalInvestigations: Full anterior pituitary hormone assessment with attention to ACTH and TSH axes
Morning cortisol and dynamic adrenal testing where indicated
Prolactin, which may be mildly raised or low
Assessment for diabetes insipidus (paired serum and urine osmolality, water balance)
Pituitary MRI to characterise gland enlargement and stalk thickening
Screening for associated autoimmune disease and review of checkpoint inhibitor exposure
redFlags: Pituitary apoplexy-like presentation or rapid deterioration with severe headache and acute visual loss requiring emergency assessment
Acute secondary adrenal insufficiency needing urgent glucocorticoid replacement
Progressive visual field defect from optic chiasm compression
Checkpoint inhibitor-associated hypophysitis with evolving hormone deficiency during cancer therapy
reference.prognosis: The inflammatory mass often regresses spontaneously or with anti-inflammatory treatment, but hormone deficiencies (especially of the adrenal and thyroid axes and diabetes insipidus) can be permanent and require ongoing replacement; outcome depends on the extent of gland damage.
pitfalls: Mistaking the inflammatory mass for an adenoma and proceeding to unnecessary surgery
Overlooking early corticotroph failure and risking adrenal crisis
Failing to consider the diagnosis in patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors
Not screening for associated autoimmune conditions
